lessons.title: The coast and early European contact
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 2 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the arrival of the Portuguese on the coast
Explain the origin of the name Cameroon
Describe the trade between Europeans and coastal peoples such as the Duala
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the date of the Portuguese arrival (about 1472), the origin of the name, the role of the Duala and the term comey. The timeline shows 1472, 1807, 1845 and 1884 as milestones.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: The first Europeans to reach the coast were the **Portuguese**, in the **1470s**. Their sailors were exploring the coast of Africa. According to tradition, they entered the estuary of the **Wouri** and were amazed by the number of **prawns** (*camarões*), so they named it **Rio dos Camarões**, the 'River of Prawns'. From this name came **Cameroon**. Other Europeans, such as the Dutch, British and French, followed.

blocks.caption: Contact with Europe
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1450 to 1900 with four dates: 1472, 1807, 1845 and 1884.

blocks.title: Coastal trade
blocks.md: Europeans traded with the **Duala**, Isubu, Bakweri and other coastal peoples. They bought **ivory**, **palm oil and kernels**, timber and, in the early period, **slaves**, and sold **cloth, guns, gunpowder, iron goods, alcohol, salt** and beads. Ships anchored in the estuary and the trade was conducted from boats or from houses on the shore.

blocks.title: Middlemen
blocks.md: The coastal rulers acted as **middlemen**: they controlled trade between European ships and the peoples of the interior, buying goods inland and selling them to Europeans at a profit. They also collected dues from ships (a payment known as **comey**), and kept the interior markets from direct European access. Wealth and power grew for the Duala leaders, and some Duala learned English and, later, German.

Trading also brought **new ideas**: Christianity, schools and new tools. But it also brought **wars** over trade, the spread of **alcohol and guns**, and, in the slave-trade era, great suffering. The coast became more important to Europeans in the 19th century, when trade in palm oil grew and European governments began to seek influence along the coast.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Portuguese arrived by sea in the 1470s; German rule began only in 1884.
- Africans were active partners and rulers in coastal trade, not only passive recipients.
- The name 'Cameroon' came from Portuguese, not from the people of the coast.

blocks.title: Example 1: the name
blocks.statement: Explain how Cameroon got its name.
steps: Portuguese sailors found many prawns in the Wouri estuary.
They called the river Rio dos Camarões.
The name changed through other languages to Cameroon.
blocks.answer: From Rio dos Camarões, the River of Prawns.

blocks.title: Example 2: why middlemen made a profit
blocks.statement: Explain how the Duala made a profit as middlemen.
steps: They bought goods from the interior cheaply.
They sold them to Europeans at a higher price.
They also collected dues from ships.
blocks.answer: By buying inland, selling at a higher price and collecting dues.

lessons.title: The Atlantic slave trade and its abolition
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 2 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain its causes and effects on Africa
Explain the movement to abolish the trade
Describe the legitimate trade that followed
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the date of the 1807 Act and the 1830s abolition of slavery in the British Empire, the named abolitionists (Equiano, Wilberforce), the role of Freetown, and the sensitivity of the topic; no casualty figures are given.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: From the 1500s to the 1800s millions of Africans were captured, forced onto ships and taken across the Atlantic to work on **plantations** (sugar, cotton, tobacco) in the Americas. The trade is called **triangular** because ships sailed from Europe to Africa carrying goods, from Africa to the Americas carrying enslaved people (the terrible **Middle Passage**), and from the Americas to Europe carrying sugar, cotton and tobacco.

blocks.caption: The Atlantic triangle
blocks.alt: A triangle between Europe, Africa and the Americas with arrows marked goods, enslaved people and sugar and cotton.

blocks.title: Causes
blocks.md: European owners in the Americas needed cheap labour for large plantations. Europeans offered **guns and goods** for captives. Some African rulers and traders took part, often through wars and raids, for wealth and for guns to defend themselves, while many people were seized against their will. Coastal ports in the Bight of Biafra and the Gulf of Guinea were part of this trade.

blocks.title: Effects on Africa
blocks.md:
- **Loss of people** and suffering of families; many young men and women were taken.
- **Wars, raids and insecurity**, and the spread of firearms.
- **Weakening of some societies**, with fear and mistrust.
- Some coastal middlemen grew rich, but many communities suffered.
- Effects in the Americas and Europe: the growth of plantations and wealth, and the creation of African-descended communities.

**Abolition.** People such as the freed African **Olaudah Equiano**, British campaigners (the Quakers and **William Wilberforce**), enslaved people who rose in revolt, and changing economic ideas pushed for an end to the trade. **Britain banned its slave trade in 1807** and ended slavery in its empire in the 1830s; the Royal Navy patrolled the coast to stop slave ships. Freed captives were settled in places like **Freetown**. Africans now sold **palm oil, ivory, timber** and groundnuts: this was called **legitimate trade**.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- The trade was a terrible crime against humanity; discuss it respectfully.
- Abolition was gradual: laws, patrols and later colonial rule did not end all slavery at once.
- The effects varied from place to place; historians still debate the numbers and details.

blocks.title: Example 1: triangle
blocks.statement: Name the three sides of the triangular trade and what each carried.
steps: Europe to Africa: guns and goods.
Africa to the Americas: enslaved people.
Americas to Europe: sugar, cotton and tobacco.
blocks.answer: Europe→Africa: goods; Africa→Americas: captives; Americas→Europe: plantation products.

blocks.title: Example 2: legitimate trade
blocks.statement: What was 'legitimate trade' and why did it grow after 1807?
steps: The slave trade was banned by Britain.
Europeans still wanted goods and Africans sold palm oil and ivory.
That trade in products replaced trade in people.
blocks.answer: Trade in goods such as palm oil instead of in people.

lessons.title: Missionaries, explorers and the scramble for Africa
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 2 — to be checked against the official text

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why European missionaries came to the Cameroon coast
Describe the work of Joseph Merrick and Alfred Saker
Explain the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 and the scramble for Africa
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: dates (Saker 1845, Victoria 1858, Berlin Conference 1884–85), Merrick's arrival (1840s), Heinrich Barth's journeys (1850s) and the balance of positive and negative effects of missions.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: In the 19th century Christian **missionaries** from Europe and the West Indies came to the coast. The Baptist missionary **Joseph Merrick**, born in Jamaica, worked at Bimbia from the 1840s. **Alfred Saker**, from England, settled at Douala in **1845**. In **1858** Saker founded **Victoria** (now Limbe) as a settlement for freed slaves and converts. The missionaries opened **schools**, **clinics** and **printing** work, translated the Bible into the **Duala** language, and taught new crafts and ideas.

blocks.caption: Missionaries and the scramble
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1840 to 1890 with 1845, 1858 and 1884 and the Berlin Conference period.

blocks.title: Effects of the missions
blocks.md: **Positive**: schools, literacy, health care, new skills and the spread of Christianity, and writing local languages down. **Negative or debated**: missionaries sometimes criticised African customs, and the missions helped European influence to spread. Mission education produced the first African teachers, clerks and church leaders.

**Explorers and traders.** European explorers such as the German scholar **Heinrich Barth** crossed the north in the 1850s, and others explored rivers and mountains. Their maps and reports gave information about land, peoples and resources. European firms from Britain and Germany set up trading posts on the coast and made agreements with local rulers. As trade grew, European governments became interested in controlling the coast.

blocks.title: The scramble and Berlin Conference
blocks.md: Between about the 1880s and 1914 European powers raced to claim African territory: the **'scramble for Africa'**. Reasons: **raw materials**, **markets**, **national pride and rivalry**, strategic bases and the 'civilising' belief. At the **Berlin Conference (1884–85)** European states agreed rules for taking African land, such as the principle of **effective occupation**. No African leaders were invited. Germany claimed **Kamerun** in 1884.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Berlin Conference did not 'divide Africa in one meeting' but set rules and settled claims; colonisation took decades.
- Explorers did not 'discover' places that Africans had known for centuries; they were new to Europeans.
- Missionaries were not all the same: some defended local rights, some did not.

blocks.title: Example 1: Saker's work
blocks.statement: Name two achievements of Alfred Saker on the coast.
steps: He settled at Douala in 1845 and began a mission.
He founded Victoria in 1858 and translated the Bible into Duala.
So: a mission, Victoria, and a Duala Bible.
blocks.answer: Founding Victoria (1858) and translating the Bible into Duala.

blocks.title: Example 2: reasons for the scramble
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why European countries wanted colonies in Africa.
steps: They needed raw materials for factories.
They wanted markets and national prestige.
So raw materials and markets (and prestige).
blocks.answer: Raw materials and markets (also prestige and strategic bases).
